title: Art History: The Big Picture
objective: After this level you can describe the big eras of art from cave paintings to today.
summary: The oldest known art is a hand stencil at least 67,800 years old, far older than writing. Art then moved through big eras, Stone Age to modern, each answering the last.

cards.headline: The oldest known artwork is a hand. It's at least 67,800 years old.
cards.body: Someone on Muna island, in Indonesia, pressed a hand to a cave wall and blew red ochre over it. Lift the hand away and its outline stays on the bare rock. It's still there. Art history starts with that hand, and this level runs from there to today.

cards.fact: If all of art history were one day, writing wouldn't show up until after 10 p.m.
cards.context: Squeeze the 67,800 years since that hand into 24 hours. Writing, invented about 5,200 years ago, appears just after 10 p.m.: for more than 22 hours, people made art but wrote nothing down. The Mona Lisa, begun about 1503, arrives about 11 minutes before midnight. Most of art's story happened before anyone could write about it.

events.label: Egypt, Greece, Rome: Egypt's art serves king and gods
Western art is mostly art for the church
Italy revives ancient Greece and Rome

cards.headline: Every era answers the one before
cards.body: Eras aren't just labels; they talk to each other. Renaissance is French for "rebirth": starting in 14th-century Italy, artists revived the ideas of ancient Greece and Rome. Centuries later, photography could record the world exactly, so painting no longer had to. Modern painters, starting in mid-1800s France, threw out the old rules. Each new era is partly a reply to the last one.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level, make it this: each era answers the one before.
